newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Buba says fines for EMU sinners a must.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba says fines for EMU sinners a must.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Friday strongly backed Germany's lone call for automatic and instant sanctions against members of Europe's future single currency that fail to maintain strict fiscal discipline.

Bundesbank council member Otmar Issing told a conference of economists in Vienna that political bodies alone were unlikely to put sufficient pressure on countries to bring their fiscal houses in order.

"Sanctions should not come after a long-winded examination process which could be drawn out over several years, but should if at all possible kick in automatically if the rules of the game are not adhered to," he said.

Issing declined to comment directly on a broad agreement on Europe's so-called stability pact struck by European Union (EU) finance ministers in Dublin last night, saying he had not seen the final document.
Germany's call for automatic sanctions against fiscal overshooting inside EMU has been met with scepticism by other EU members who prefer a political control mechanism.
Officials in Dublin hinted on Friday the summit was likely to endorse a compromise that would fall well short of Germany's original demands for automatic fines on budget offenders.
"If you leave this decision to political gremiums (bodies), then you have potential sinners judging on actual sinners," he said.
"The idea is that these sanctions have a preventive effect, that the Damocles' sword of sanctions hangs over every budget debate," Issing added.
Issing said financial markets were unable to react to fiscal overspending inside Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) quickly and strongly enough.
"The effect of financial markets' sanctions will come much too late and will be much too small," he told reporters after his speech.
Issing reiterated the Bundesbank's conviction that EMU will start in 1999 as scheduled. "If politicians can't deal with that, then they have to do something about it," he said.
"Our role in this process is to defend the German mark to our last breath, that's our national cause and it is also in Europe's interest," the central bank's chief economist added.
Issing declined to speculate how many countries would qualify for joining EMU at the start.

Commenting on Germany, he said the country was still far from meeting all Maastricht criteria for EMU membership, which set strict thresholds in terms of debt, deficits, inflation, and exchange and interest rates.
"Germany at the moment is far away from meeting the three percent (deficit) goal. There's a lot that still has to be done, particularly on the fiscal side," he said.
